title: Playbook Check CLI Commands (BLD-678)
description: This tour walks through the addition of two new CLI commands — `hlx playbook check <rule-ref>` and `hlx playbook checks <rule-ref>` — that form the client-side interface to the Playbook feature introduced in BLD-675/676. The changes follow the existing `goals/` command group pattern and introduce the first polling loop in the CLI: POST to trigger a check, then repeatedly GET status until a terminal state (PASS, FAIL, ERROR) is reached or a 10-minute timeout expires. All changes are additive: three new files and one new switch case in the top-level dispatcher.

steps.description: The top-level CLI dispatcher imports the new `runPlaybook` router from `src/playbook/index.ts`. This mirrors every other command group (goals, tickets, etc.) and is the single entry-point registration needed to make `hlx playbook` reachable.
steps.title: Step 1 — Dispatcher: import the new playbook router

steps.description: A new `case 'playbook':` block is added to the main switch statement using the same `configOrHelp` pattern as `goals`. When the user types `hlx playbook ...`, control flows immediately to `runPlaybook()` in `src/playbook/index.ts`. The usage text is also updated here to surface both new subcommands to users running `hlx --help`.
steps.title: Step 2 — Dispatcher: register the 'playbook' case

steps.description: This file is a structural clone of `src/goals/index.ts`. It extracts the first positional argument as the subcommand name, dispatches `check` to `runCheck` and `checks` to `runChecks`, and falls back to printing help text for unknown inputs. Error handling uses `parseApiError` (imported from `goals/utils.ts`) so HTTP and network errors are surfaced with user-friendly messages, consistent with the rest of the CLI.
steps.title: Step 3 — Playbook router: command group entry point

steps.description: Rather than duplicating error-formatting logic, the playbook router imports `parseApiError` directly from `src/goals/utils.ts`. This is a deliberate reuse decision noted in the code review: all command groups share the same error presentation layer, keeping user-facing error messages consistent.
steps.title: Step 4 — Reuse parseApiError from goals/utils

steps.description: Three module-level constants define the polling contract: `POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 5_000` (5 seconds between GETs), `MAX_POLLS = 120` (capping total wait at 10 minutes), and `TERMINAL_STATUSES = new Set(['PASS', 'FAIL', 'ERROR'])`. The `CheckRecord` interface mirrors the server's `PlaybookRuleCheck` model fields so TypeScript catches any API shape drift at compile time.
steps.title: Step 5 — check.ts: constants and CheckRecord type

steps.description: The command resolves the `<rule-ref>` argument to a rule ID, then POSTs to `/playbook/rules/${ruleId}/check` using `hxFetch` with `basePath: '/api'`. This matches the server's API route prefix exactly. The response body contains the newly-created check record (including its `id`), which is immediately passed into the polling loop. If the returned status is already terminal (e.g., an org-level ERROR), the loop exits on the first iteration.
steps.title: Step 6 — check.ts: POST to trigger the check

steps.description: This is the first polling pattern in the helix-cli codebase. The loop GETs `/playbook/rules/${ruleId}/checks/${checkId}` every 5 seconds. On each iteration it checks whether `check.status` is in `TERMINAL_STATUSES`. If yes, it breaks and prints the result. If `MAX_POLLS` is reached without a terminal state, a clear timeout message is printed and the process exits with code 1. Exit code 0 is reserved for PASS; all other terminal states exit 1, enabling CI integration.
steps.title: Step 7 — check.ts: GET polling loop

steps.description: After the polling loop resolves, the command prints interpretation text, compliance counts (compliant/violating/total), compliance rate, and representative examples from the check result. The `--json` flag bypasses all formatting and dumps the raw `CheckRecord` as JSON — useful for scripting and CI pipelines, consistent with the pattern in `goals/get.ts`.
steps.title: Step 8 — check.ts: result formatting and --json flag

steps.description: This file handles `hlx playbook checks <rule-ref>`: it GETs `/playbook/rules/${ruleId}/checks` and renders a formatted table (ID, Status, Compliance %, Checked At) using `padEnd` alignment — the same technique as `goals/list.ts`. An empty list is handled gracefully with a human-readable message. The `--json` flag returns the raw array. No polling is involved here; this is a simple read command.
steps.title: Step 9 — checks.ts: list check history

steps.description: All changes in this ticket are purely additive: three new files (`src/playbook/index.ts`, `src/playbook/check.ts`, `src/playbook/checks.ts`) and one new `case` block in `src/index.ts`. No existing command logic was modified. The polling loop is self-contained in `check.ts`. Error handling, flag parsing, and HTTP communication all reuse existing shared utilities (`parseApiError`, `hxFetch`, `hasFlag`, `getPositionalArgs`), ensuring zero regression risk on existing commands and a consistent developer experience across the CLI.
steps.title: Step 10 — Summary: additive changes, clean code paths
